samples.text:
In today's society, many students go to university. Some people say that the main aim of university is to prepare students for a job, but others think it should be a place where people can learn knowledge for its own sake. This essay will discuss both opinions.

Firstly, people who think university is for employment have strong reasons. University education is very expensive and many students take a loan to pay the fees. So they expect to find a good job with high salary after graduation. Also, companies need workers who has practical skills, for example in engineering, medicine or computer science. If universities only teach theory, the graduates will not be ready for work and the economy will suffer.

Secondly, other people believe that university should be a place for learning any subject which students are interested in. Subjects like history, philosophy or literature does not lead directly to a job, but they help people to think critically and understand the world. In addition, many important discoveries in science was made by researchers who were only curious and did not think about money. If universities focus only on jobs, this kind of research may disappear.

In my opinion, I think both purposes are important, but preparing for employment should be the main purpose. Most of students go to university because they want a better career, and it is fair that universities help them. However, universities should still keep some space for pure knowledge and research.

In conclusion, some people think universities are for jobs, and others think they are for knowledge. Although both views have advantage, I believe employment is the main purpose, but knowledge for its own sake should not be forgotten.
samples.why: Both views covered and an opinion given · supporting points relevant but general · repetitive conclusion · mechanical linking (Firstly, Secondly, Also) · adequate vocabulary · several agreement and article errors.

samples.text:
Universities today face competing expectations. Many people see them primarily as training grounds for the workforce, while others insist that their true value lies in the pursuit of knowledge for its own sake. Although I accept that employability matters, I believe universities should not be reduced to vocational institutions.

Supporters of the employment-focused view make a reasonable case. Higher education has become costly, and students who graduate with considerable debt understandably want courses that lead to secure, well-paid work. Employers, too, frequently complain that graduates lack practical skills such as teamwork, project management or familiarity with industry software. From this perspective, a university that ignores the job market is failing both its students and the wider economy.

On the other hand, there are strong arguments for protecting learning that has no immediate practical purpose. Disciplines such as philosophy, history and pure mathematics develop the ability to analyse complex problems, question assumptions and communicate ideas clearly, qualities that are valued in almost any career. Moreover, much of the research that has transformed modern life began as curiosity-driven enquiry, with no commercial application in mind at the time. If funding and teaching are directed only towards what is currently profitable, society risks losing the foundations of future innovation.

In my opinion, the two goals are less opposed than they first appear. A literature student can still gain transferable skills through internships and careers guidance, while an engineering student benefits from exploring the ethical and historical context of their field. Universities should therefore offer practical preparation without abandoning there commitment to independent thought.

To conclude, while preparing graduates for employment is an important function of universities, I believe it should not be the main or only one, since the pursuit of knowledge itself brings long-term benefits to individuals and to society.
samples.why: Clear position maintained · both views developed with relevant examples · well-organised paragraphs with clear topics · good range of collocations · frequent error-free sentences with one minor slip.

samples.text:
The role of higher education has become increasingly contested as tuition costs rise and labour markets change. One camp holds that a university exists chiefly to equip students for employment; another maintains that it should be a place where knowledge is pursued for its own sake. In my view, a university that sacrifices the latter in favour of the former undermines what makes it distinctive.

It is easy to see why the employment argument resonates. For most undergraduates, a degree represents a substantial financial commitment, and it is reasonable for them to expect that it will improve their career prospects. Governments that subsidise higher education likewise want a return on that investment in the form of skilled professionals, whether doctors, engineers or data analysts. Seen in this light, courses detached from the needs of the economy can appear to be an expensive luxury.

However, this view rests on a narrow conception of usefulness. Many of the capabilities employers prize most, such as the capacity to evaluate evidence, construct an argument and adapt to unfamiliar problems, are cultivated precisely through open-ended academic study rather than job-specific training. Furthermore, skills tailored to today's labour market may be obsolete within a decade, whereas a deep understanding of a discipline endures. At the level of society, fundamental research undertaken without any commercial aim has repeatedly laid the groundwork for later technological breakthroughs.

For these reasons, I believe the pursuit of knowledge should remain at the heart of a university's mission, with employability treated as a valuable by-product rather than the overriding objective. This does not mean ignoring students' career needs; work placements and professional guidance can sit comfortably alongside rigorous academic study. What should be resisted is the notion that a subject is worthwhile only if it leads directly to a particular job.

In conclusion, although universities clearly have a role in preparing people for work, their deeper and more enduring purpose is to advance and share knowledge, which ultimately serves both individuals and the economy better.
samples.why: Both views fully explored with extended, well-supported reasoning · clear, nuanced position · logical progression and well-managed paragraphs · sophisticated, precise vocabulary · wide range of structures, virtually error-free.
